title: Michael: date, subtitle and purpose
short: Written at Town End, Grasmere, October to December 1800, and printed as the last poem of Lyrical Ballads (1800), subtitled 'A Pastoral Poem'.
body: Dorothy Wordsworth's Grasmere Journal records William walking up Greenhead Ghyll 'in search of a sheepfold' on 11 October 1800 and labouring at the poem through the autumn; it closed the second volume of Lyrical Ballads (dated 1800, issued January 1801). Sending the volume to Charles James Fox, Wordsworth explained that 'Michael' and 'The Brothers' were meant to show the domestic affections of the Lake District 'statesmen', small independent landowners whose class he thought was 'rapidly disappearing'. To Thomas Poole he described the poem as a study of a strong-minded man torn between two passions, love of his child and love of his inherited land. The subtitle claims the classical genre of pastoral while replacing its idealized singing shepherds with a real working one. The opening addresses a walker leaving 'the public way', so that the reader enters the story as the poet did, by noticing a heap of stones.

title: Green-head Ghyll
short: A steep stream-ravine running up from Grasmere towards Fairfield; 'ghyll' is a northern word for a narrow wooded or rocky gully.
body: 'Gill' or 'ghyll' comes from Old Norse gil, a deep ravine with a stream, and survives in Lake District and Yorkshire place-names; the gh- spelling is a literary form that Wordsworth helped to fix. Greenhead Ghyll rises behind the village of Grasmere towards the fells of Fairfield. The Fenwick note (1843) says that the sheepfold on which the poem turns 'remains, or rather the ruins of it', and that the family of Luke had once owned the house at Town End where the Wordsworths lived. The brook is called 'tumultuous' and 'boisterous' at the beginning and at the end (ll. 2, 6, 484), so the poem is framed by the same untamed water, a sign of nature continuing while the human story ends.

title: the heap of unhewn stones
short: The unfinished sheepfold, introduced before its story: the poem begins and ends with this easily overlooked ruin.
body: The narrator insists that the stones are something 'you might pass by, / Might see and notice not': Wordsworth's characteristic claim that the humblest object can carry the deepest history. The heap is the remnant of the fold Michael began with Luke (ll. 387-425) and left unfinished at his death (l. 474), so the reader sees the end before the beginning. A sheepfold in these mountains is an unroofed stone enclosure in which sheep are gathered, here beside a brook. Dorothy's journal for 11 October 1800 adds that the fold they found was 'built nearly in the form of a heart unequally divided', a detail critics have read as the hidden emblem of the poem.

title: 'Homely and rude': pastoral in blank verse
short: The narrator apologizes for a plain, unadorned tale, in line with the Preface's choice of 'low and rustic life' and ordinary language.
body: 'Homely' means domestic and plain; 'rude' means unpolished, not discourteous. The disclaimer is partly conventional modesty, but it also states a programme: the 1800 Preface to Lyrical Ballads argues that rural life shows the 'essential passions of the heart' in a simpler and more durable form, and that poetry should use 'a selection of the real language of men'. The poem is in unrhymed iambic pentameter, the metre of Milton and of serious narrative, so the plain tale is given epic dignity.

sources.cite: Wordsworth, Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800; revised 1802)

title: 'my second self'
short: Wordsworth imagines future young poets of the hills continuing his work after his death: the poem is itself a kind of inheritance.
body: 'Second self' translates the classical alter ego, used of a true friend (Cicero, De amicitia 80). Here it describes poetic succession: the tale is told 'for the delight of a few natural hearts' and for youthful poets who will carry on the poet's way of feeling about these hills. The idea quietly parallels the main story, in which Michael wants Luke to be his second self on the land and fails. The poet's legacy, a story handed on, survives where the shepherd's legacy, land and fold, does not. Critics have often noted that the poem is as much about the transmission of feeling as about property.

title: Michael
short: The name of the archangel lends the shepherd a patriarchal, Old Testament weight.
body: Michael is the archangel who fights for God's people (Daniel 12:1; Revelation 12:7), and the name carries biblical authority into a story whose scenes repeatedly recall Genesis: an old father, a son of his old age, a heap of stones as covenant, a son lost in a far country. The phrasing 'There dwelt a Shepherd, Michael was his name' has the formula of a ballad or of scripture (compare Job 1:1, 'There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job'). Wordsworth makes him eighty and more, of 'unusual strength', and keen in mind: a heroic figure of the ordinary.

title: the South wind's 'subterraneous music'
short: Michael reads the weather like a text: the south wind's low roar warns him of storms, compared to distant bagpipes.
body: 'Subterraneous' means underground; the wind among the fells makes a deep, muffled sound, which the comparison to Highland bagpipers makes both strange and homely. The passage shows Michael's skill as a kind of knowledge of nature that others lack ('When others heeded not'), the practical counterpart of the poet's own attentiveness. His remark 'The winds are now devising work for me!' turns weather into a fellow-worker. The idea that the hills 'like a book' preserve his memories (l. 70) continues this theme of the landscape as a written record.

title: the fields 'like a book'
short: The land is a record of Michael's life, preserving the memory of his work and of the animals he saved.
body: Wordsworth's letter to Fox makes the same point in prose: the statesman's attachment to his small inheritance is bound up with his domestic affections. In the poem the fields and hills hold 'so many incidents' of hardship, skill and courage, and so attach his affections to the place itself. The passage ends in a famous phrase for this bond: 'A pleasurable feeling of blind love, / The pleasure which there is in life itself.' 'Blind' here means instinctive, below reasoning, not foolish. The theme prepares us for the tragedy: losing the land would mean losing the book of his life.

title: Helpmate
short: Isabel is introduced in the language of Genesis, the wife as 'help meet' for the man.
body: In Genesis 2:18 God says, 'I will make him an help meet for him', meaning a helper suitable for him; the two words fused into 'helpmeet' and 'helpmate'. Isabel is twenty years younger than Michael, and her spinning wheels (one for wool, one for flax) mean the household never stops working. Wordsworth gives her a mind of her own: her silent memory of Richard Bateman (ll. 259-271) shapes the plan to send Luke away, and her fear that 'if thou leave thy Father he will die' (l. 299) is the poem's quiet prophecy.

title: a mess of pottage
short: A dish of thick soup or porridge; the phrase also recalls Esau, who sold his birthright for a 'mess of pottage'.
body: 'Mess' is a serving of food, and 'pottage' a thick broth of oats or vegetables, the plain fare of a hill-farm. The expression was proverbial from the story of Esau, who sold his birthright to Jacob for bread and pottage (Genesis 25:29-34; the phrase 'mess of pottage' itself comes from older English Bibles and chapter headings, not the KJV text). Wordsworth may intend only the literal supper, but the echo is suggestive in a poem about whether an inheritance will be sold.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Genesis 25:29-34

title: card
short: To card wool is to comb out and straighten its fibres with toothed boards before spinning.
body: Cards were pairs of boards set with wire teeth; the wool was drawn between them to make soft rolls for the spindle. The list of evening tasks (carding, mending sickle, flail and scythe) shows father and son as working partners, and the domestic economy is completed by the Housewife at her wheel. The detail matters to the poem's argument: the family's 'endless industry' (ll. 94-95) is self-sufficient, the life of independent producers that Wordsworth told Fox was disappearing.

title: THE EVENING STAR
short: The cottage is named after the lamp that burned late in its window, visible across the valley.
body: The 'aged utensil' of a lamp, hung under the huge chimney-hood, becomes 'a public symbol' of the couple's thrift and industry, and the neighbours call the house after it. The evening star (Venus as Hesperus) is the first light of evening, appropriate to the late-life family and their son born in Michael's old age. Wordsworth's Fenwick note admits the name actually belonged to another house further north in the valley. Near the end the name returns in capitals: the cottage 'Is gone' and the ploughshare has passed over its site (ll. 478-479), so the light becomes an emblem of what has been extinguished.

title: Easedale and Dunmail Raise
short: Real places around Grasmere: Easedale is a side valley to the west; Dunmail Raise is the pass north towards Keswick.
body: Easedale runs north-west from Grasmere village; Dunmail Raise is the road over the watershed between Grasmere and Thirlmere, marked by a large cairn that local legend makes the burial place of Dunmail, the last king of Cumbria, defeated by the English king Edmund in 945 (the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Edmund's harrying of Cumbria that year). The names fix the poem in the Wordsworths' own landscape: they lived at Town End, below these slopes, and the Fenwick note says Luke's family once owned their house. The topography makes the light of the Evening Star visible to the whole vale.

title: 'female service'
short: Michael has nursed and rocked his baby son 'as with a woman's gentle hand', unusually for fathers of his time.
body: Wordsworth emphasizes that this tenderness was not mere play, 'as is the use / Of fathers', but deliberate care 'with patient mind enforced'. The passage complicates the picture of the stern patriarch: the father's love is maternal as well as paternal, and it explains why the separation is catastrophic. The son is both the object of his love and his hope for the future of the land.

title: the Clipping Tree
short: The great oak under which the sheep were sheared; 'clipping' is the northern word for shearing.
body: Wordsworth's own note of 1800 glosses it: 'Clipping is the word used in the North of England for shearing.' The oak 'Stood single', like the cottage, and its 'matchless depth of shade' made it the shearers' shelter. It is a communal place where the child learns the work, and it returns at the very end: the cottage is gone, 'yet the oak is left / That grew beside their door' (ll. 481-482). The tree, like the sheepfold, outlives the family and keeps a dialect name that 'yet it bears', an example of the landscape preserving local memory.

title: 'Two steady roses that were five years old'
short: The healthy red cheeks of a five-year-old boy, an unusual and tender variant on a conventional image.
body: Rosy cheeks are a commonplace of ballad and pastoral, but Wordsworth makes them 'steady' (lasting, not a passing flush) and dates them precisely, as if counting the years of growth. At this age Michael makes Luke a shepherd's staff from a sapling and sets him at gaps to turn the flock, 'Something between a hindrance and a help'. The gentle comedy of the passage keeps the narrative close to the shepherd's affectionate view of his son.

title: surety for his brother's son
short: Michael had guaranteed his nephew's debts; when the nephew failed, Michael became liable for a sum close to half his property.
body: To stand 'in surety' is to promise to pay another's debt if he defaults; the 'forfeiture' is the penalty now due. Scripture warns repeatedly against it: 'He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it' (Proverbs 11:15; compare 6:1-2). Wordsworth keeps the nephew's guilt ambiguous ('if he were false... if he were not false', ll. 237-238), so the disaster arises from economic chance rather than villainy. Michael's anguish is that he has become 'a fool at last / To my own family', and his first thought, selling part of the land, is rejected because he could not 'lie quiet in my grave' if it passed to a stranger.

title: patrimonial fields
short: Land inherited from his fathers: the poem's central value, which Michael will risk his son to keep free of debt.
body: Wordsworth told Poole that Michael is moved by two strong affections, love of his child and love of landed property, including the feelings of inheritance and family independence. The fields were 'burthened' (encumbered with debt) when they came to Michael, and only by long labour did he clear them (ll. 375-377). His solution, sending Luke to a prosperous kinsman in trade so the land 'shall be free' (l. 245), sets the two loves against each other. Critics have debated whether the poem endorses this choice or quietly exposes its cost; the narrator never blames Michael, but the outcome makes the land and the son mutually destructive.

title: Richard Bateman
short: A poor parish-boy who grew rich overseas and built a marble-floored chapel; usually identified with Robert Bateman, benefactor of Ings chapel near Kendal (rebuilt 1743).
body: Isabel's example is the parish-boy Richard Bateman, who goes to London, is sent overseas by his master, grows 'wondrous rich' and leaves money to the poor and a marble-floored chapel in his birthplace. The story is usually linked with Robert Bateman, a merchant at Leghorn (Livorno) born in the Staveley district, who paid for the rebuilding of Ings chapel in 1743 and died suddenly the same year, leaving his executors to finish it. Dorothy Wordsworth's journal for 6 October 1802 describes the chapel's marble floor. Isabel's memory supplies a hopeful model of the poor boy who goes out and makes good; the reader may sense the darker possibility that Bateman died far from home.

title: parish-boy
short: A pauper child maintained at the cost of the parish under the Poor Law.
body: Under the English Poor Laws each parish was responsible for its own destitute; a 'parish-boy' was an orphan or child of poor parents supported or apprenticed by the parish officers. The detail of a collection at the church door ('shillings, pence / And halfpennies') shows the neighbourly charity of the dale, and the purchase of a pedlar's basket shows how a boy might begin in trade. The story's appeal to Isabel lies in the contrast: if a parish-boy could rise, Luke with kinship and means behind him should do still better.

title: the corner-stone and the covenant
short: Michael asks Luke to lay the first stone of the sheepfold as a pledge between them, in the manner of the covenant-stones of Genesis.
body: In Genesis 31:44-52 Jacob and Laban gather a heap of stones as a witness: 'This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness'; Jacob also sets up a stone as a pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28:18-22) and Joshua sets up stones as a memorial (Joshua 4:6-7). Michael's 'corner-stone' recalls Psalm 118:22. The stone is to be a sign Luke will remember in temptation, and Michael promises to build on while he is away. The episode is the emotional climax; the covenant fails on the son's side but not on the father's ('I shall love thee to the last'), and the stones themselves outlast both.

title: the 'dissolute city' and the prodigal
short: Luke falls into 'evil courses' in the city and flees abroad, a prodigal son who never returns.
body: The narrative of Luke's decline is told in five lines, deliberately brief. The son's name and story recall the parable of the prodigal son in Luke 15:11-32, who 'wasted his substance with riotous living' in 'a far country'; but in Wordsworth's version there is no homecoming. The city is the counter-world to the dale throughout Wordsworth's poetry of 1800, the place where, as the Preface says, the 'increasing accumulation of men in cities' blunts the mind. 'Beyond the seas' implies escape from justice or debt, perhaps transportation.

anchor: never lifted up a single stone
title: 'And never lifted up a single stone'
short: The poem's most famous line: on many days the old man went to the fold and did nothing, overwhelmed by grief.
body: The line reports village belief ('tis believed by all'), not the narrator's observation, so grief is seen from outside, with tact. Matthew Arnold's essay on Wordsworth (1879) singles out this kind of plain, unheightened line as characteristic of Wordsworth's best manner. The plainness contrasts with the preceding sentence on the 'comfort in the strength of love', which can make a loss endurable: Michael continues his labour for seven years, but the unmoved stone measures what love cannot repair.

title: the ending: the estate sold
short: Isabel dies three years after Michael; the land goes 'into a stranger's hand', the cottage is ploughed under, and only the oak and the ruined fold remain.
body: The final lines fulfil Michael's fear (l. 231) word for word, 'a stranger's hand'. 'Great changes have been wrought / In all the neighbourhood' points to the historical subject Wordsworth named in the Fox letter: the decline of the statesmen and the consolidation of small farms. The poem ends where it began, at 'the boisterous brook of Green-head Ghyll', closing the circle around the unfinished sheepfold, whose remains are now the only monument and the reason for the poem's existence.
